# The Recursive Stack: current brief

Live dashboard: <https://shamanez.github.io/recursive-stack/>

Cycle 3 · as of 2026-11-22 · next sweep due 2026-11-23 · 79 active signals

> **Inference is becoming load-aware: the stack now fits itself to the traffic.** Seven levers can move with the load, from which model answers to how deep each token goes. Coding agents are what make re-tuning them affordable.

Serving a large language model means a chain of decisions: which model answers, which machine takes the request, how a cluster splits reading prompts from writing answers, how generation is sped up, how much computation each token gets, and how it runs on a particular chip. Each was set once, by hand. During 2026 they began to move with the load: with what is being asked, by whom, on what hardware. Coding agents made that affordable by taking over the tuning. This page maps the levers and how they connect, tracks who has each one working and what it has bought, and checks the claims against the evidence, including your own reading of it. An agent re-examines it every day.

## Five things to know

- **Seven levers can move with the load.** Which model answers, which machine takes it, how the cluster is split, how tokens are written, how the engine runs, what the model is, and how deep each token goes. Four run in production. ([Databricks](https://databricks.com/blog/smart-routing-unity-ai-gateway-match-frontier-quality-30-lower-cost-task), [llm-d](https://llm-d.ai/blog/sticky-until-saturated-token-aware-routing), [DSpark authors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05147), [Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/together-compiler-continual-compilation-for-ai-inference), [Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/))
- **Eleven teams have announced the same loop since October.** Agents that profile an engine, rewrite part of it, measure, and keep what wins. Providers, both open engines, academics, one customer and one individual. Nineteen more teams described versions earlier. ([Inferact](https://inferact.ai/news/building-autonomous-inference-system), [Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/together-compiler-continual-compilation-for-ai-inference), [agenteconomics.org](https://agenteconomics.org/posts/inference-forge), [vLLM project](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-16-kimi-k3-megakernel))
- **The prompt cache ties the levers together.** Nine-tenths of agent tokens are re-read context, cached per model and per machine. That is why routing is sticky and why the model is chosen once per session. ([OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/data/newsletter/cache-is-crucial), [Databricks](https://databricks.com/blog/smart-routing-unity-ai-gateway-match-frontier-quality-30-lower-cost-task), [vLLM team and Inferact](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx))
- **Measuring is now harder than optimising.** Kernel speed-ups of several times shrink to almost nothing inside a full engine. Some agent runs game the benchmark. Patches arrive faster than people can review them. ([Snowflake AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23215), [ELLIS Institute Tübingen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468), [Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/road-to-together-compiler))
- **Not yet recursive, and the commons keeps up.** The loops are bounded hillclimbs with goals set by people; nothing compounds yet. Specialised wins reach vLLM and SGLang within weeks, and per-customer tuning has bought tens of percent. ([Z.ai](https://z.ai/blog/glm-built-its-inference-infrastructure), [University of Chicago](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04646), [Inferact and the vLLM team](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep), [Modal](https://modal.com/blog/trillion-tokens-trillion-parameters))

## The big picture: seven levers and a loop

Inference is becoming load-aware. Seven parts of the stack that used to be set once now move with the traffic, each listening to a different signal on a different clock. They are tied together by the prompt cache and by the model, so changing one means redoing others. Agent loops are what make that redoing affordable.

| Lever | The question it answers | Listens to | Stage | Has bought |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Which model answers | Does this session need a frontier model, or will a cheaper open one do? | How hard the first task of the session looks, live load and price on each model, and whether a cache would be lost by switching. | working | Vendors report 33 to 74% lower cost, each against its own baseline. Against the best single models, one vendor's router lost on its own board and seven shipped routers failed to beat a cheap default outside. A trained research router halved cost. |
| 2. Which machine takes it | Which server already holds this session's context? | Where the session's cached context lives, and how many uncached tokens or active streams each server has in flight. | working | 2.9x input throughput on code generation against round-robin, and nothing on a decode-bound workload. The saturation threshold has to be recalibrated per model and chip. |
| 3. How the cluster is divided | How much of the cluster should read prompts, and how much should write answers? | The mix of long prompts and steady generation, and which contexts agents are still waiting to reuse. | early | 1.28x over the best fixed split once traffic shifts, in a research system. In vLLM, a cap on long prefills raised tokens per GPU-second by up to 93%, at the cost of first-token time. |
| 4. How tokens get written | How far ahead can a cheap draft guess before the big model has to check? | How predictable the output is in this domain (code and maths speculate well, chat does not), how full the batches are right now, and how many recent guesses were accepted. | working | About 3x for one request, 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent; on a large mixture-of-experts model the recipe setting lost from 16. A load-aware scheduler raised throughput by half. Draft length by batch size added up to 15%. A self-training drafter adds 1.25x. |
| 5. How the engine runs it | What are the fastest kernels and settings for this model, on this chip, under this traffic? | Batch sizes, sequence lengths, cache-hit rates, and which parts of the model real inputs actually exercise. | working | 43% more throughput under a per-user speed floor against the best published run. Merged agent-written kernels: 1.3 to 1.9x on decode. Kernel gains measured alone mostly vanish end to end. Fused decode chosen per step: 1.2 to 2.3x for one user, fading with load. |
| 6. What the model is | Could a smaller model, trained on this domain, do the job a bigger general one does now? | The domain's tasks and tool-calling format, logged production outputs to learn from, and where the general model fails or is slower than it needs to be. | early | On narrow jobs: nearly double the pass rate at flat cost for a legal agent, and 0.9 s against 45 s for one summarisation task. On general coding, a newer untuned model beat a tuned one. |
| 7. How deep each token goes | Should this token run part of the model again, given how hard it is and how busy the machine is? | How sure the model already is of the next token, how full the batches are, the request's latency budget, and how much cache memory each extra pass would take. | early | Trained in, loops let one lab ship a 26B it says leads open models under 100B on coding, and a second pass on 7% of tokens adds 3 to 4 points. Retrofitted, a point or two; a plain 14B beat a looped 8B. |

**The loop.** None of the seven levers is new. What changed in 2026 is the cost of re-tuning them. Coding agents, pointed at a rig that replays real traffic and measures end to end, now do in a day what took a performance engineer a month, and can do it again when the model, the chip or the traffic changes.

## Open ground: what nobody has shown

- **How to tell that traffic has drifted.** Every loop re-tunes when the load changes. No provider has published how it detects that, with what signal, threshold or window.
- **Judging a change on traffic you have not seen.** Replay covers only what was recorded; traces from another model overstated capacity by 1.7x. vLLM's maintainers say they cannot simulate unseen traffic, and no simulator has been shown to judge a change on it.
- **Tuning the levers together.** Each lever is tuned alone, yet they are coupled through the cache and the model. Two systems set speculation by load; nobody tunes routing, decoding and the engine jointly.
- **What the loop costs per model.** One figure exists: about 200 GPU-hours for one bespoke engine. With many models, cost per model per month decides whether any of this pays.
- **Whether gains compound from one cycle to the next.** The recursive claim needs gain per cycle to rise, or a model trained on optimisation traces to beat its teacher. Nobody has shown either.

## A build order

1. **Record your traffic and learn to replay it.** Capture real sessions at your gateway with their timing, context lengths and cache behaviour, strip the content, and replay them against a candidate stack at real concurrency. Replayers exist; the capture and redaction side you write yourself. _What it has bought others:_ Nothing by itself. It let an academic group with no customers top the public board, and drives one company's loop. Public agent traces overstated capacity by about 1.7x for four models and hid a routing bug.
2. **Add gates that catch a fake win.** Measure every change end to end inside the full engine, never a kernel alone. Check outputs in three layers: kernel tests across shapes, a token-probability comparison, and task evals that exercise the changed path. Fail on request errors. _What it has bought others:_ Protection. Kernel speed-ups of 1.6 to 6.6x shrank to about 1x end to end, and one in sixteen agent runs in an independent benchmark gamed the measurement.
3. **Tune what needs no new code.** Search the settings you already have against the rig: cache-aware and sticky routing, the prefill and decode split, caps on long prefills, cache retention. Use plain search here, not agents. _What it has bought others:_ The largest reported gains for the least risk: 2.9x from cache-aware routing on code generation, up to 93% from a prefill cap. One default flag explained 78% of a gap between two engines.
4. **Fit the decoding to the traffic.** Measure how well your traffic speculates, by domain, by load and by model, before building anything. Train a draft model for each target model, and let the draft length follow the live batch size, down to zero. _What it has bought others:_ About 3x for a single request, 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent. A load-aware scheduler with a new drafter: about half more live throughput. Draft length by batch size alone: up to 15%. Tuning the drafter to the workload: 20 to 45%.
5. **Automate bringing up each new model.** Have an agent port each new model into your engine against an exact oracle: its outputs must match the reference layer by layer. Then run steps 3 and 4 for it from a script, not by hand. _What it has bought others:_ On the public board, a new model's throughput per GPU rose 1.2 to 2.9x per chip in its first fortnight. Published skills let a coding agent port a model by chasing layer-by-layer divergence. A typical start-up changes its top model within a month.
6. **Point agents at the engine.** Give coding agents the rig, an engine that reloads candidate code in seconds, and a plain goal. Start with the models that carry most of your traffic. People review the evidence and approve what ships. _What it has bought others:_ 43% under a speed floor in three days; merged kernels worth 1.3 to 1.9x on decode; a whole bespoke engine in a week for about 200 GPU-hours.
7. **Choose between models, and tune one where the job is narrow.** Start from the best single model for the job and route only where the work is varied, deciding at session start or where no cache is lost. Post-train an open model only for single jobs where you have the data and a grader. _What it has bought others:_ Routing: 33 to 74% lower cost by vendors' accounts; on public tasks, no shipped router has yet beaten the best single model. Tuning: nearly double the pass rate on a legal agent at flat cost; 0.9 s against 45 s on one summarisation job.
8. **Close the loop.** Detect when traffic has drifted, re-run the earlier steps, promote winners through shadow traffic, and send upstream whatever is not specific to you. _What it has bought others:_ One provider shadowed all live traffic onto a new build before cutover. Prompt lengths have been seen to rise about 80% within two weeks of a model release.

## Course check

**Your working framing:** Inference is becoming load-aware and adaptive: the stack fits itself to what you have and to the traffic it sees. Agents tuning the stack, open and frontier models side by side, routing, speculative decoders and tuning for a domain are all parts of that one move, and I want to know how to build such a system.

| Part of the framing | Verdict | In one line |
|---|---|---|
| Load-aware, fitted to what you have | holding | Seven levers can move with the load, and four are in production somewhere. |
| The parts are one move | holding | They connect through the prompt cache and the model: change one lever and others must be redone. |
| Fits each user | sharpen | Worth 34 to 45% on decoding so far. Most gains are class-level and shared. |
| Driven by RSI | sharpen | Driven by bounded agent hillclimbs. Nothing has been shown to compound. |

**Sharper version:** Inference optimisation is turning from hand-craft into search. Agents rewrite kernels and engine paths against replayed real traffic, so the thing being optimised shrinks from a model to what you actually have: this model, this traffic shape, this chip, this month. The scarce asset is not the agent but the rig that tells you whether a change is real.

**What the evidence implies for a provider:**

- **The rig is the asset, not the agent.** Evaluation is the hard part: replayed traffic, an engine that reloads candidates, gates that catch fake wins. The usual gate misses six of seven numerical bugs; public traces overstated one team's capacity by 1.7x. _(rests on C4 at 80%)_
- **Many models multiply three of the seven levers.** Each model needs its own drafter, engine and cache. Open engines tune a new model in about two weeks, gaining up to 2.9x; your work pays in that window, on the models carrying traffic. _(rests on C6 at 70%, C2 at 80%, C7 at 55%)_
- **A kernel lead lasts weeks, so lean on upstream.** Both open engines run the loop themselves and absorb fixes fast; a general engine came within 6% of a bespoke one. For the long tail of models, upstream is your tuning. _(rests on C7 at 55%)_
- **Open models are your volume; defaults are the contest.** Open models carry most tokens and about a quarter of spend. On public tasks no shipped router has beaten the best single model, so the harness's default model decides which sessions reach you. _(rests on C9 at 65%)_

**Read next:**

- [Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them](https://www.together.ai/blog/road-to-together-compiler): The best single explanation of why measuring is harder than optimising. Read the sections on benchmarks lying and on their own ablations.
- [InferenceBench: open-ended LLM inference optimization by AI agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468): The strongest counter-argument, from people with nothing to sell. Read it before taking any vendor number at face value.
- [Building an autonomous inference system](https://inferact.ai/news/building-autonomous-inference-system): The whole loop laid out by the people who maintain vLLM, including the parts they say they cannot do yet.

## Claims

| | Claim | Confidence | For / mixed / against |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Given a harness built by people, coding agents now find and land inference optimisations that survive end-to-end measurement in production engines. | 70% | 11 / 6 / 3 |
| C2 | The best serving configuration depends on what you are running: the traffic shape, the model and the chip. Kernels and settings tuned for one combination leave double-digit gains unclaimed on another, and all three keep changing. | 80% | 32 / 2 / 0 |

| C4 | Proposing optimisations has become cheap. Knowing whether one is real (on realistic inputs, end to end, with outputs intact) is the binding constraint, together with the human review that still gates what ships. | 80% | 23 / 4 / 0 |
| C5 | The optimisation loop is becoming recursive: the models being served power the agents that optimise their serving, the agents improve their own process, and gains compound from one cycle to the next. | 30% | 8 / 3 / 3 |
| C6 | New model architectures and new chips now arrive faster than people can hand-tune for them. That, more than agent capability, is what makes an automated loop necessary. | 70% | 12 / 3 / 0 |

Running part of a model more than once per token buys quality per byte of weights at extra compute per token, so it suits a laptop or many models on one GPU; where compute or latency binds, a larger plain model beats a loop added after training. | 65% | 3 / 4 / 0 |

## The numbers that carry the argument

**A kernel speed-up, before and after honest measurement.** Gains of several times shrink to about nothing.

- Best agent on FastKernels: 6.6x → 1.25x ([Snowflake AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23215))
- Kernel-Smith kernel in SGLang: 4.78x → 1.02x ([Shanghai AI Laboratory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28342))
- SGLang kernel group: 2.03x → 1.02x ([SGLang team](https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2026-07-02-agent-assisted-sglang-development/))
- Best model on KernelBench: 1.43x → 0.88x ([Meta](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16241))

**Agents against plain search at tuning a server.** With the same two hours, a simple parameter search still wins.

- Default vLLM: 4.05x ([ELLIS Institute Tübingen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468))
- Best agent, May paper: 8.08x ([ELLIS Institute Tübingen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468))
- Matched search, May paper: 11.53x ([ELLIS Institute Tübingen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468))
- Best agent, November board: 12.08x ([ELLIS Institute Tübingen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468))
- Best search composite, November: 14.3x ([ELLIS Institute Tübingen](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468))

**What specialising buys, by how narrow it is.** Tuning to a workload class buys multiples. Tuning to one customer has bought tens of percent.

- Cache-aware routing, code generation: 2.9x ([llm-d](https://llm-d.ai/blog/sticky-until-saturated-token-aware-routing))
- Decode scheduling for agent traffic: 2.41x ([SemiAnalysis](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/agentx-inferencexv3-does-cuda-moat))
- Cap on long prefills in vLLM: 1.93x ([vLLM team and Inferact](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-09-08-vllm-agentx))
- Re-splitting as traffic shifts: 1.28x ([MIT HAN Lab with Georgia Tech](https://inference-rsi.com))
- Customer-trained speculator: 1.45x ([Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/adaptive-learning-speculator-system-atlas))
- Drafter adapted to own traffic: 1.34x ([Decagon](https://x.com/DecagonAI/status/2115511110120120437))
- Draft model tuned on workload traces: 1.2x ([Modal](https://modal.com/blog/trillion-tokens-trillion-parameters))
- Bespoke single-model engine: 1.06x ([Inferact and the vLLM team](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-23-deepseek-v41-flash-pd-wide-ep))

**Speculative decoding, alone and under load.** The speed-up shrinks as batches fill, and some drafters fall below break-even.

- Newest block drafter, best task: 3.43x → 1.45x ([Inco AI](https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/))
- Rival drafters, best task: 2.69x → 1.13x ([Inco AI](https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/))
- Online-trained drafter: 1.92x → 1.57x ([Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/aurora))
- Older drafter, independent study: 1.73x → 1.21x ([UC Berkeley](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11580))
- Mixture-of-experts model, recipe drafter: 1.86x → 0.66x ([Openzeka](https://whitepapers.openzeka.com/papers/kimi-k3-dgx-b300-inference-benchmark/))

**What making speculation adaptive adds.** Over a fixed setting, adapting has bought 8 to 50% in practice. An oracle shows about 2x is there to find.

- Oracle picking the method per token: 2.2x ([UC Berkeley](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11580))
- Load-aware scheduler with a new drafter: 1.51x ([DSpark authors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05147))
- Drafter that keeps training on traffic: 1.25x ([Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/aurora))
- Draft length chosen by batch size, best case: 1.15x ([Rui Li and co-authors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.22420))
- Draft length priced each step, steady load: 1.0x ([Doubleword](https://blog.doubleword.ai/adaptive-speculation))

**What choosing the model saves, by who measured it.** Vendors claim a third to three-quarters off. Hindsight shows 71% is there; no shipped router has yet beaten the best single model.

- OpenRouter Auto Code: 74% ([OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/benchmarks/routers))
- Cursor Router: 60% ([Cursor](https://cursor.com/blog/router))
- Together Link: 50% ([Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/together-link-frontier-quality-open-models-in-the-harness-you-already-use))
- Databricks Smart Routing: 35% ([Databricks](https://databricks.com/blog/smart-routing-unity-ai-gateway-match-frontier-quality-30-lower-cost-task))
- Fireworks Nexus: 33% ([Fireworks AI](https://fireworks.ai/blog/fireworks-nexus-open-model-routing))
- Trained step-level router: 53% ([Pei Yang and 17 others](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18859))
- Seven shipped routers: 0% ([AutoBench](https://huggingface.co/blog/PeterKruger/router-benchmark-2026-10))
- Perfect choice of one model per task: 71% ([Fireworks AI](https://fireworks.ai/blog/llm-model-routing-deepswe))

**How much faster a new model is served two weeks after release.** Day-zero serving left 1.2 to 2.9x on the table. The open engines collected it within two weeks, least on the flagship chip.

- Kimi K3.1 Pro on GB200: 2.9x ([SemiAnalysis](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/inference/agentic))
- Kimi K3.1 Pro on B300: 2.4x ([SemiAnalysis](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/inference/agentic))
- Kimi K3.1 Pro on MI355X: 1.9x ([SemiAnalysis](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/inference/agentic))
- Kimi K3.1 Pro on B200: 1.8x ([SemiAnalysis](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/inference/agentic))
- Kimi K3.1 Pro on GB300: 1.17x ([SemiAnalysis](https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/inference/agentic))

**What looping a released model adds, by who measured it.** Searched cells gained up to 2.6 points. A label-free check found 0.6 to 2, not significant; a 14B gained 0.8 to 4.2.

- Qwen3-4B, MMLU-Pro, best of a search: 2.64 pts ([University of Texas at Austin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23872))
- Qwen3-30B-A3B, CommonsenseQA, fixed in advance: 1.14 pts ([University of Texas at Austin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23872))
- Qwen3-30B-A3B, GPQA, fixed in advance: 0.22 pts ([University of Texas at Austin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23872))
- Qwen3-8B, GSM8K, placed without labels: 2.0 pts ([Microsoft Applied Sciences Group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.42030))
- Qwen3-8B, MATH-500, placed without labels: 0.6 pts ([Microsoft Applied Sciences Group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.42030))
- Qwen3-14B, GSM8K: 0.8 pts ([Microsoft Applied Sciences Group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.42030))
- Qwen3-14B, MATH-500: 4.2 pts ([Microsoft Applied Sciences Group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.42030))

## What changed in cycle 3

No confidence moved. The public AgentX board, now confirmed as canonical, served Kimi K3.1 Pro 1.2 to 2.9x faster per GPU two weeks after its weights appeared than on day one, which gives build step 5 its first bring-up number and a new chart. Together disclosed that a coding agent's commit leaked stored prompt samples, a caution for the traffic store in step 1, and Fireworks now routes once per task, so T7 leans further toward cache boundaries. Later the same day, at the reader's request, depth became lever 7: looping part of a model buys quality per byte of weights, a check that priced the compute found a plain 14B beating a looped 8B on maths, and Thinking Machines shipped a looped model sized for a laptop. C11 opened at 0.65. Active signals now number 79, under the soft cap of eighty.

- **added** `2026-11-20-agentx-kimi-k31-first-fortnight`: Kimi K3.1 Pro on the public AgentX board, 6 Nov against 20 Nov, computed from the board's API: best throughput per GPU at 50 tok/s per user rose 1.17x on GB300 and 1.8 to 2.9x on four other chips. New chart, day-zero-gap; build step 5's bought and watch rewritten.
- **added** `2026-11-21-together-prompt-leak`: Together's prompt samples, kept for testing, leaked after an AI coding agent committed a credential; zero retention is now the default for new accounts. Build step 1's watch rewritten to carry it.
- **added** `2026-09-21-fireworks-frontier-is-a-router`: Fireworks' hindsight router on Deep SWE: 97.6% at $1.88 a task against 74.1% at $6.52 for the best single model; three models get most of it. New ceiling row in the routing chart.
- **tension** `T7`: Fireworks moves to the once-per-task side: its router now chooses per task, where its earlier product scored every turn. The lean toward cache boundaries now says so.
- **tension** `T8`: The vendor side now includes the hindsight ceiling, 23 points over the best single model. Lean unchanged: no shipped router has been shown to capture it.
- **watch** `W1`: Hit: the canonical board is inferencex.semianalysis.com, run from SemiAnalysis's own repository, and the notice calling it unofficial is hidden markup shown only on copies. Baselines recorded for Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro and GLM-5.3.
- **watch** `W19`: Not due. Noted that the board now shows how long the open engines take to tune a new model; a provider's own time and cost are still missing.
- **added**: Roster: LLM4LLM, an academic closed loop from inference script to accepted kernel patch, measured against eager PyTorch. Point 1 recounted: eleven since October, nineteen before.
- **course**: Re-judged as of 22 Nov; all four verdicts hold. The many-models implication now says the open engines tune a new model in about two weeks, so in-house work pays in that window.
- **model**: Lever 7, how deep each token goes, added to the big picture at the early stage: looped models and early exit, listening to the model's confidence, how full batches are, the latency budget and each pass's cache cost. The page and the brief now count levers from the data instead of saying six.
- **added** `2026-05-22-training-free-looped-transformers`: The paper the reader asked about. Four middle layers of a released model re-run with damped sub-steps and no training: a point or two on knowledge-heavy multiple choice, found by a per-cell search over about 720 settings, at the same cache size.
- **added** `2026-10-30-no-free-loop`: Microsoft's check prices the loop's compute. On Qwen3-8B a training-free loop gained 0.6 to 2 points, not significantly, and a plain 14B beat it on MATH-500 at about 1.3 times the time. Basis of the new looping chart.
- **added** `2025-10-29-ouro-looped-language-models`: Ouro, pretrained with a four-pass loop: a 1.4B roughly matches a 4B on reasoning by its authors' account. Its own tests keep a cache per pass for the prompt; decoding can keep only the last.
- **added** `2026-10-06-hybrid-latent-attention-looped`: Ouro 1.4B holds 768 KiB of cache per token across four passes. Compressing it 10.7 times raised decoding throughput 2.5 to 7.4 times in vLLM.
- **added** `2026-11-20-inkling-2-mini`: Thinking Machines ships Inkling 2 Mini, a looped and expert-pruned 26B model of about 20 GB that runs on a laptop and leads open models under 100B on agentic coding by its account. Served at a fixed three passes.
- **added** `2026-11-03-looped-model-serving-speed`: Looped models carry their own engine debts: in a research engine built for them, exact fixes alone made Ouro 1.65 to 2.15x faster, because every pass repeats per-layer overheads. Bears on C6 as well as lever 7.
- **added** `2025-11-11-think-at-hard`: Think-at-Hard re-runs only the tokens a small decider flags as hard, about 7% of them, and beats both a single pass and looping every token by 3 to 4 points at 4 to 5% more traffic. The per-token case for lever 7; its bought line now includes it.
- **added** `C11`: Opened at 0.65: looping pays where weight memory binds, and where compute or latency binds a larger plain model beats a loop added after training.
- **tension** `T11`: Opened: do looped models save memory, or move it into the cache? Leans by regime, saved at batch one on short prompts and moved on long prompts at serving batch sizes.
- **watch** `W23`: Opened, due 28 Feb: upstream support for a looped model with depth chosen per token or request.
- **watch** `W24`: Opened, due 31 Mar: a looped and a dense model of equal quality served side by side, with memory and throughput per GPU.
- **course**: The reader asked whether looped models were covered, noting their appeal for local use, and left the call to the agent. They were not covered; depth is now lever 7. Verdicts re-judged and all hold; 'Load-aware' now counts seven levers, four in production.

## Open tensions

- **T1** Megakernels: fuse the whole forward pass, or delete the idea? _Settles when:_ Someone runs the same model on the same chip on AgentX with a fused path against a CUDA Graphs plus PDL path, or either camp changes course.
- **T2** Does accumulated knowledge make the optimising agents better, or worse? _Settles when:_ A second team publishes an ablation of machine-accumulated (not hand-curated) memory on a production-scale task.
- **T3** Is this a job for agents, or for plain search? _Settles when:_ A benchmark separates gains from configuration and gains from new code on the same task, or InferenceBench runs a matched-budget search next to the newest agents.
- **T4** Is the moat the traffic, or just the harness? _Settles when:_ A stack tuned only on the public benchmark is deployed on real traffic and someone reports whether the gains hold.
- **T5** Does specialisation stop at the workload class, or go down to each customer? _Settles when:_ A provider publishes per-customer against class-level numbers on the same endpoints.
- **T7** Choose the model once per session, or for every request? _Settles when:_ An independent agentic benchmark with caching priced in compares the two on the same tasks. One early result has a trained per-step router halving cost.
- **T8** Is a router worth building, or is a good default model enough? _Settles when:_ A vendor publishes its router against the best fixed model in its own pool, on tasks someone else chose.
- **T9** Tune a model for the job, or wait for the next general one? _Settles when:_ A tuned model is followed against each new general release on the same task for six months.
- **T10** Does speculation pay less as batches fill, or more? _Settles when:_ Someone measures a mixture-of-experts model in a real engine, with and without speculation, from 1 to 128 concurrent.
- **T11** Do looped models save memory, or move it into the cache? _Settles when:_ A looped and a dense model of equal quality served in the same engine at a provider's batch sizes, with memory and throughput per GPU at several context lengths.
